stimuli.text: A block of mass 4 kg on a 20° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 7 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.1. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.5 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.07\cos(5t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) and a solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.9 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 2x^2$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 1$$ m to $$x = 3$$ m?

options.why: The force is not constant.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 60 N/m and 70 N/m are connected in series and support a 4 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Correct. k_eq = k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).
The force is the weight, mg.
Both springs share the load.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.

questions.stem: Masses of 10 kg and 1 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
Use T = m₂(g + a).

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 70$$ N/m is compressed 0.07 m and launches a 0.4 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Take the square root.
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
The ½ appears on both sides.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1.1 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.
I = mL²/3.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 120 kg load 27 m at constant speed in 10 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: P = W/t.
That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.
Correct. P = mgh/t.

questions.stem: A 2 kg cart moving at 8 m/s collides with and sticks to a 7 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: The carts share the momentum.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.

questions.explanation: v_f = 2·8/9 = 1.78 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 49.8 J.

questions.stem: A 46 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward at 4 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Check the direction of the acceleration.
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Include gravity.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).

questions.stem: A car moving at 14 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 8 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

options.why: Δx = v₀²/(2a).
Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0.
That is the stopping time in seconds.
Divide by 2a, not a.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 40 m is banked so that a car at 29 m/s needs no friction. What is the banking angle?

options.why: Use tan θ = v²/(rg), from dividing the force components.
Correct. tan θ = v²/(rg).
Square the speed.
Measure the angle from the horizontal.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = -1t^3 + 4t^2 + 1t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its velocity at $$t = 2$$ s?

options.why: Recheck the arithmetic.
Correct. Differentiate once: v = 3at² + 2bt + c.
The constant term c is part of the velocity.
That is the position; differentiate it.

questions.explanation: v(t) = -3t² + 8t + 1, so at t = 2 the value is 5.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 40° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction acts up the slope.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 22 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 19 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Recheck the average.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -16x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.
T = 2π/ω.
ω is the square root of the coefficient.
Correct. ω = √16 = 4 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 2x^3 - 12x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Take the square root.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 6x² − 12 = 0 gives x = 1.41 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A uniform 6 m beam weighing 600 N rests on supports at both ends. A 700 N load sits 2 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
The load is not at the center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.
Include the beam's weight at its center.

questions.stem: A 1.4 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 45$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: The ratio is m/k.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
Include the 2π.
That is the frequency.

questions.stem: A 2000 kg car heading east at 10 m/s collides with a 1000 kg car heading north at 17 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Weight each velocity by its mass.
Divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: A planet has 2 times Earth's mass and 3 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: The ratio is inverted.
Correct. g ∝ M/R².
g decreases with radius.
g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.

questions.stem: A 0.9 kg ball hits a wall at 18 m/s and rebounds at 2 m/s. The contact lasts 0.08 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Divide by time.
Include the rebound.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.4 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.19$$ kg/s. What is the time constant of its approach to terminal speed?

options.why: τ = m/b.
Correct. From m dv/dt = mg − bv, τ = m/b.
That is the terminal speed.
τ has units of seconds: m/b.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 20.6 m/s and τ = m/b = 2.11 s.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 5 m down a 30° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction removes energy.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 400$$ N/m is compressed 0.24 m and launches a 0.3 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
Take the square root.
The ½ appears on both sides.

questions.stem: A 4 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 1 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
I/R² = M/2.
For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 8.71 m/s².

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 4 kg and radius 0.4 m spins at 7 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 0.5 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Use rotational inertias, not masses.
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
The clay's inertia is mR².
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.

questions.stem: What is the rotational inertia of a uniform rod of mass 1 kg and length 3 m about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod?

options.why: The mass is spread along the rod.
That is about the center.
That is a disk's formula.
Correct. I = ML²/3 (parallel-axis theorem from ML²/12).

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 9 m high at 7 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Fall time is √(2h/g).
Take the square root for the time.
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 2 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 1.6$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 2 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
½Iω² = W; solve for ω.
W = ½Iω².
Convert revolutions to radians.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 4t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 3 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its velocity at $$t = 2$$ s?

options.why: Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.
That is the position.
Include the initial velocity.
Correct. Integrate a(t) and add the initial velocity.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 4$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^3$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
The rod is not uniform.

questions.stem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 1.1 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
Some energy goes into rotation.
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅖MR².

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$1 \times 10^{22}$$ kg and radius $$9 \times 10^{6}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.

questions.stem: A 2 kg ball moving at +5 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 1 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 1 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: That would be a sticking collision.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
Kinetic energy is conserved too.
Only equal masses exchange velocities.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = 1.67 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 6.67 m/s.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 2.7 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
The weight acts at L/2.
τ = MgL/2.
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.

questions.stem: A 3 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 4 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.3. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Friction opposes the motion.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Include friction on the table block.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 7 rad/s and amplitude 0.15 m. What is its speed when it is 0.045 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Use A² − x² under a square root.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.

questions.stem: A 4 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 3t^2$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 2$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Integrate the force over time.
Divide by the mass to get speed.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
The force is not constant.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 8 N·s; v = J/m = 2 m/s.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 25 m/s at 20° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its maximum height?

options.why: Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
H = (v₀ sin θ)²/(2g).
Use the vertical component, v₀ sin θ.
Only the vertical component matters.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 23.5 m/s, v₀y = 8.55 m/s. H = v₀y²/(2g) = 3.73 m.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 16 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: T² ∝ r³.
Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).
The exponent is 3/2.
Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).

questions.stem: A 10 g bullet moving at 370 m/s embeds in a 3.8 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: h = V²/(2g).
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.

questions.explanation: V = 0.971 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.0481 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 4 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 0.5 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.07 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.

rubric.example: solid sphere: 5.16 m/s; solid cylinder: 4.98 m/s

parts.prompt: Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
